title: Quarterly vs. Annual Calendar for Carpet Low-Moisture Encapsulation: Frequency by Foot Traffic and Annual Spend
seoTitle: Carpet Encapsulation Calendar: Quarterly vs Annual Frequency & Cost
metaDescription: Carpet low-moisture encapsulation calendar by foot traffic: monthly, quarterly, or annual at $0.10–$0.25/sq ft per pass. Model annual spend in our calculator.
excerpt: Office managers learn how to match low-moisture carpet encapsulation frequency to measured foot traffic, from monthly lobby passes to once-a-year private offices. The guide converts each schedule into annualized dollars per square foot so you can budget and audit vendor proposals.
quickAnswer: Most US offices should schedule low-moisture carpet encapsulation quarterly in main corridors, monthly in entry lanes and break-area walk-offs, and once or twice a year in private offices. Expect $0.10–$0.25 per sq ft per pass, which puts a 10,000 sq ft mixed-traffic office at roughly $4,000–$7,500 per year when zones are scheduled separately instead of treating the whole floor the same.

blocks.text: Why Frequency Matters More Than the Per-Pass Price

Low-moisture encapsulation works by applying a crystallizing polymer detergent, agitating it with a cylindrical or orbital pad machine, and letting the dried residue trap soil so it releases on the next vacuuming. The process uses roughly a tenth of the water of hot-water extraction, so carpet is typically walkable in 30 to 60 minutes. That speed is what makes it attractive for interim maintenance, but it also creates a scheduling trap: encapsulation only removes soil that your nightly vacuuming can then pull out. If you wait too long between passes, embedded grit cuts fibers, traffic lanes gray permanently, and no interim method will restore them.

The right calendar is therefore set by soil load, not by habit. A carpet that sees 2,000 footsteps a day in a reception lane needs a fundamentally different cadence than the carpet under a VP's desk. Vendors who quote one frequency for the entire floor are either overspending your budget in quiet zones or under-servicing the lanes that drive replacement cost.
Foot-Traffic Thresholds That Set the Calendar

Facility managers can estimate traffic without counters. Use badge-swipe data, headcount per zone, and proximity to entrances, elevators, restrooms, and coffee stations. The thresholds below reflect what carpet mills and IICRC-trained floor technicians generally treat as light, medium, and heavy commercial use.

blocks.text: These annual figures assume $0.10–$0.25 per sq ft per pass, which is the range most US janitorial and specialty floor contractors bid for encapsulation on commercial glue-down or tile carpet with routine furniture. Smaller jobs sit at the top of the range because mobilization, chemical prep, and a project minimum (commonly $250–$450 for specialty floor work, well above the $90–$135 per-visit minimum used for routine janitorial visits) get spread over fewer square feet.

The most cost-effective programs split the floor into two to four zones and stagger them across the year. Heavy lanes get a monthly pass, the open field gets four passes timed to seasonal soil peaks, and private offices get a single pass before the holiday slowdown. In northern climates, schedule an extra lane pass in late March to remove ice-melt residue; in the Sun Belt, add one after summer pollen and dust season.

items.name: Map zones on the floor plan
items.text: Color-code heavy, medium, and light zones and measure each in square feet. A typical 10,000 sq ft office breaks down as roughly 1,000 sq ft heavy, 2,000 sq ft medium-heavy, 5,000 sq ft medium, and 2,000 sq ft light.

items.name: Assign passes per zone
items.text: Apply the table: 12 passes for heavy, 6 for medium-heavy, 4 for medium, and 1 for light. Total annual pass-square-feet in the example is 12,000 + 12,000 + 20,000 + 2,000 = 46,000.

items.name: Price the pass-square-feet
items.text: At $0.10–$0.16 per sq ft for a mid-size floor, 46,000 pass-square-feet equals about $4,600–$7,360 per year, or $383–$613 per month if amortized.

items.name: Pair with hot-water extraction
items.text: Plan one restorative extraction per year in heavy and medium-heavy zones. Encapsulation residue and deep oily soil eventually need flushing, and most carpet warranties expect periodic extraction.

items.name: Lock the calendar into the contract
items.text: Write the zone map, pass counts, and target months into the scope so the vendor cannot quietly drop passes or bill unscheduled work orders.

blocks.title: Benchmark: amortized floor program
blocks.text: National benchmarks put a quarterly deep floor program at $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month when amortized. A zoned encapsulation calendar that lands far above $0.06 per sq ft per month across the whole floor usually means light zones are being serviced too often; one far below $0.03 usually means heavy lanes are being neglected.
Comparing Flat Schedules vs. Zoned Schedules

To see why zoning saves money, compare three common approaches on the same 10,000 sq ft floor. A flat monthly schedule buys 120,000 pass-square-feet per year, overservicing 70 percent of the carpet. A flat quarterly schedule buys 40,000 pass-square-feet but leaves entry lanes soiling for 13 weeks between passes, which accelerates permanent graying and shortens carpet life by years. Zoned scheduling targets the soil where it actually accumulates.

blocks.caption: Annual spend on a 10,000 sq ft office at $0.10–$0.16 per sq ft per pass

blocks.text: The zoned model costs only slightly more than flat quarterly service while giving heavy lanes twelve passes instead of four. With commercial carpet tile replacement running several dollars per sq ft installed, extending the life of just the 3,000 sq ft of traffic lanes by two or three years pays for the program several times over.
Daily Practices That Stretch the Interval

Encapsulation intervals depend heavily on what happens between passes. The crystallized residue only leaves the carpet when it is vacuumed, so a weak nightly vacuuming routine can make a quarterly schedule perform like an annual one.

items: Require nightly HEPA vacuuming of heavy zones and at least twice-weekly vacuuming of medium zones; specify CRI Seal of Approval equipment in the scope.
Install 10 to 15 feet of walk-off matting at every exterior entrance; matting can capture a large share of tracked-in soil before it reaches carpet.
Spot-treat coffee and soda spills within 24 hours with a neutral-pH spotter so sugars do not wick back up after encapsulation.

Stage carts properly: a three-shelf janitor cart such as the Rubbermaid Commercial 6173 with 8-inch wheels and a 300 lb shelf capacity keeps pads, spotters, and encapsulant jugs organized without dragging gear across fresh carpet.
Use a dolly like the Rubbermaid Brute 5-caster twist-lock unit, rated to 250 lb, for moving barrels of trash off the carpet path instead of sliding them, which grinds soil into fibers.

Keep hard-floor chemistry off carpet: neutral-pH concentrates like Fabuloso Professional diluted at 1:64 are suited to VCT and restroom floors, but residue tracked onto carpet attracts soil, so mop edges carefully at carpet transitions.

blocks.title: Safety Data Sheets and slip control
blocks.text: Encapsulation chemistry falls under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, so vendors must keep current SDS sheets on site and train technicians. Although carpet dries quickly, require wet-floor signage at carpet-to-hard-floor transitions until the surface is fully dry, and confirm the vendor's certificate of insurance names your company or landlord as additional insured.
How to Write the Frequency Into Your Contract

A frequency calendar is only enforceable if it is written into the scope of work. Spell out zone square footage, number of passes per zone per year, target months, the encapsulant product or a Green Seal equivalent, and a verification method such as a signed completion log with date-stamped photos. If you pay a flat monthly retainer, divide the annual cost by 12 and itemize it as a line so you can confirm the vendor is not banking the money while skipping passes.

For routine janitorial pricing, remember that monthly costs are calculated with 4.333 weeks per month. A vendor that bills a carpet program as a weekly line item should convert it correctly; 52 weeks divided by 12 months equals 4.333, not 4. A weekly $100 carpet line is about $433 per month, not $400.

faqs.q: Is quarterly carpet encapsulation enough for a typical office?
faqs.a: Quarterly is right for open workstation areas and conference suites with moderate traffic, roughly 150 to 400 crossings per day. It is not enough for entry lanes, reception, and elevator lobbies, which usually need monthly passes. Most offices land on a zoned calendar where the average works out close to quarterly but the heavy lanes get much more attention.

faqs.q: Can encapsulation replace hot-water extraction completely?
faqs.a: No. Encapsulation is an interim maintenance method. Plan at least one hot-water extraction per year in heavy and medium-heavy zones to flush accumulated polymer residue and oily soil. Many commercial carpet warranties require documented periodic extraction, so keep vendor invoices and completion logs as proof.

faqs.q: How do I convert an encapsulation calendar into a monthly budget line?
faqs.a: Add up the pass-square-feet for the year, multiply by the per-pass rate, and divide by 12. For example, 46,000 pass-square-feet at $0.12 equals $5,520 per year, or $460 per month. If a vendor quotes weekly spot work, convert it using 4.333 weeks per month so the line matches your calendar.

faqs.q: What should a vendor provide before starting carpet encapsulation?
faqs.a: Ask for a current certificate of insurance listing your company or landlord as additional insured, SDS sheets for the encapsulant and spotters under OSHA HazCom, proof of technician training, and the product's Green Seal or CRI listing if your building has green cleaning requirements. Also confirm whether furniture moving and after-hours access are included or billed separately.

faqs.q: Does carpet tile change the recommended frequency?
faqs.a: The traffic thresholds are the same for broadloom and carpet tile, but tile lets you swap out the worst lane tiles instead of encapsulating more often. Many managers keep a stock of attic tiles and rotate entrance tiles annually, which can stretch heavy-zone intervals from monthly to every six weeks.
